name: Trip.com Group Limited

profile.description: Trip.com Group, founded in 1999 as Ctrip and now headquartered in Singapore, is China's largest online travel agency and a growing global platform. Its brands include Ctrip, Qunar, Trip.com and Skyscanner, covering hotels, air and rail ticketing, packaged tours and corporate travel [3]. Q2 2026 net revenue was RMB15.7B (+6% YoY), and international platform revenue grew more than 50%. The quarter also absorbed a one-time RMB5.18B penalty from China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) for abuse of a dominant market position [1].

innovation.label: STRONG
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): Trip.com has expanded beyond its China base. International platform revenue grew more than 50% YoY in Q2 2026, and inbound travel revenue grew at a high double-digit rate [1]. Revenue grew from RMB18.3B in 2020 to RMB60.7B in 2025 [3]. AI Deployment (2/2): Trip.com ships its TripGenie AI assistant and rolled out fully AI-powered search across the platform in Q2 2026. AI-assisted orders through TripGenie reportedly rose ~400% YoY, with nearly 60% of interactions booking-related [5]. Market Share (2/2): Trip.com is the dominant Chinese OTA. SAMR's penalty explicitly found a dominant market position [1]. Pipeline (1/2): CEO Jane Sun's four-stage AI travel framework (inspiration, search, transaction, fulfillment) gives direction but no dated product launches [5]. R&D Intensity (1/1): R&D runs at 24.3% of TTM revenue (RMB14.7B in 2025), which is top-quartile for online travel [2][3].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): Trip.com's stated mission of 'pursuing the perfect trip for a better world' is specific to travel and connects it to a broader purpose. The SAMR ruling on abusive distribution practices undercuts how well that mission is lived [1][6]. Community Impact (1/2): The company publishes annual ESG reports, highlighting 16M+ users choosing low-carbon travel options and a CEO-led ESG committee, but cites no dollar-quantified community programs [6]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention data was found, and two co-founders departed at the start of 2026 [7]. Insider Buying (0/2): As a foreign private issuer, Trip.com files no Form 4 data, and no insider buying was found.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Scored mechanically on the Growth template. D/E is 16.9%, and the 5-year revenue CAGR is 27.1% (RMB18.3B in 2020 to RMB60.7B in 2025, flattered by the COVID-depressed base) [2][3]. TTM net margin of 37.0% is inflated by large non-operating investment gains: pretax margin is 46% against a 16% operating margin [2]. TTM ROE of 14.6% sits just below the 15% target. Q2 2026 revenue growth slowed to +6% YoY in RMB [1]. Forward P/E of ~10.8 is self-derived from FMP's TTM P/E-implied share price (~RMB293) over FY2027 consensus EPS of RMB27.11 [2][4]. Forward PEG of ~0.84 is also self-derived (10.8 over a 12.9% FY2026-FY2028 consensus EPS CAGR), because FMP's reported forward PEG is negative from the gain-inflated TTM base. Liquidity is ~$125M/day.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (5/9): Online travel agencies face real disintermediation risk from AI agents that can search and book directly with hotels and airlines. Trip.com's defense, in CEO Jane Sun's words, is that its 'proprietary travel data and supply capabilities become increasingly valuable' across the inspiration-to-fulfillment chain [5]. Its scale in China's distinct digital ecosystem adds protection. No analyst work found quantifies the risk, so it is scored as EXPOSED rather than PROTECTED. AI Opportunity (0/1): TripGenie order growth (~400% YoY) is reported, but no AI revenue figure or percentage is disclosed [5].

infinite_game.summary: Trip.com has built a durable, purpose-framed travel franchise, invests about a quarter of revenue in R&D, and is expanding internationally. However, Chinese regulators fined it RMB5.18B for abusing its dominant position through tiered distribution programs, and Sinek would recognize that as finite play: it extracted value from partners instead of strengthening the ecosystem. The departure of two co-founders in early 2026 adds organizational uncertainty [1][7].

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): 'Pursuing the perfect trip for a better world' is idealistic and service-oriented, and the company's sustainable-travel initiatives reference it [6]. The SAMR finding of partner abuse shows it is only partially lived [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): CEO Jane Sun provides leadership continuity, and the company runs a CEO-led ESG committee [6]. The early-2026 departure of two co-founders amid the antitrust probe is a stability concern [7], and no employee sentiment data was found.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): SAMR found Trip.com abused its dominant market position. The company is now dismantling its tier-one and tier-two distribution programs, which is a 'win by restricting rivals' posture, the opposite of Sinek's worthy-rival mindset [1].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Trip.com has grown from a China call-center booking agent into a global app-based platform (Skyscanner, Trip.com), with international revenue now growing >50% [1][3]. This is meaningful evolution within the same travel-intermediary model.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Trip.com keeps spending ~24% of revenue on R&D and is investing in international expansion and platform-wide AI search despite slowing domestic growth [1][2].

investment_thesis: After falling from a 52-week high of $78.99 to ~$41, Trip.com trades at ~10.8x FY2027 consensus EPS with a net-cash balance sheet (net debt/EBITDA -1.0x) and only 16.9% D/E [2][4]. The international platform is growing >50% YoY. Q2 2026 adjusted EPS of $1.07 beat consensus despite the antitrust charge, and AI-assisted TripGenie bookings are scaling quickly [1][5]. With the one-time RMB5.18B SAMR penalty now booked, the regulatory overhang is better defined.
thesis_continued: The bear case is that the SAMR ruling permanently impairs Trip.com's domestic pricing power. It must dismantle its tiered distribution programs, and core RMB revenue growth has already slowed to 6%, with ticketing down 1% [1]. Reported earnings quality is weak: the 37% TTM net margin depends on investment gains, and consensus net income for 2026 (~RMB16.7B) is roughly half of 2025's reported RMB32.4B [3][4]. Co-founder departures, US-China ADR risk, and AI-agent disintermediation in online travel add uncertainty.
key_catalysts: International platform (Trip.com, Skyscanner) sustaining >50% revenue growth and margin improvement
Successful migration of hotel partners to the new multi-tiered framework without major take-rate erosion after the SAMR decision
TripGenie and AI search lifting conversion; AI-assisted orders already up ~400% YoY
Inbound China tourism growth from visa-free policies
key_risks: Further SAMR remedies or fines restricting Trip.com's domestic distribution and commission practices
Agentic AI (search engines, LLM assistants) booking directly with suppliers and bypassing OTAs
Earnings quality: TTM net margin of 37% vs 16% operating margin, reliant on investment gains
Leadership transition risk after two co-founders departed in early 2026
